text: A model that scores brilliantly on its training data can still fail on new data, and a model that's too simple can fail on both. Understanding why is the most useful piece of theory in machine learning, because it tells you what to do when a model disappoints. Two ideas explain it: bias and variance.

Training error tells you how well the model fits rows it has already seen. Generalization is how well it performs on new rows drawn from the same source. The gap between the two is the price of having learned from a limited sample — every choice in this course, from splitting data to regularization, is about managing that gap.

Bias is systematic error — a model with high bias makes strong simplifying assumptions, like assuming the relationship is a straight line, so even with unlimited data it misses the true pattern. That's underfitting. Variance is sensitivity to the training sample — a model with high variance bends to follow the noise in whatever rows it happened to see. Give it a different sample and it produces a very different model. That's overfitting.

Noise is randomness in the data itself — no model can remove it, so some error is irreducible. Simple models sit at high bias, low variance. Flexible models sit at low bias, high variance. This is the bias-variance tradeoff — making a model more flexible lowers bias but raises variance, and the best model balances the two.

Generating 40 noisy points from a sine curve, splitting them in half, and fitting polynomials of degree 1, 3, and 9: degree 1, a straight line, is bad on both train and test — high bias. Degree 3 is good on both, with a small gap. Degree 9 has the lowest training error of all three, but the worst test error by a wide margin — the signature of high variance. If you judged models on training error alone, you'd pick the worst one.

To see variance directly, imagine collecting a fresh training set many times. Refitting each model on 200 new samples and recording its prediction at x equals 0.25, where the true value is exactly 1.0: the line's average prediction is 0.49, far from the truth — that's bias.

Degree 9 averages 0.97, nearly right on average, but its individual predictions scatter with a standard deviation of 0.59 — more than four times that of degree 3. That's variance. Degree 3 is close on both counts, averaging 1.01 with a tight spread of just 0.13.

To recap: generalization, performance on unseen data, is the actual goal. Too-simple models have high bias and underfit; too-flexible models have high variance and overfit. Training error always improves with more flexibility, so only held-out data can reveal which is which. Next up, lesson 5: how to diagnose and fix overfitting and underfitting in practice.
